highlights.title: Uncontrolled AI could lead to 'silicon species' rivalling humans, warns Microsoft
highlights.summary: Mustafa Suleyman says he believes rival AI firm Anthropic is in effect teaching Claude it "may be conscious".
body: The head of Microsoft AI has warned that without adequate safeguards, the development of AI could lead to the emergence of a new "silicon species" wich competes with humans.
Mustafa Suleyman said rival firm Anthropic is treating AI like it is human, an approach he called "misguided" which could create technology that humanity cannot control.
Speaking to the BBC's Today programme, the chief executive said it was "right" for people to be concerned about AI, but there were "very practical things that we can do" to control it.
The comments are the latest in a series of stark warnings from the AI industry about the technology's possible dangers. Anthropic has been approached for comment.

highlights.title: Iceland-based Treble raises $18 million for its voice simulation platform
highlights.summary: Treble's voice simulation platform is used by voice AI model developers, AI wearable, and robotics companies
body: Voice AI has emerged as one of the hottest sectors in AI, with investors pouring in billions of dollars to serve use cases ranging from automating customer support and sales calls to creating meeting notetakers and developing AI smart glasses that use voice as the primary interaction surface.
Meanwhile, AI labs are quickly releasing models, and hardware makers are trying to create the best experience for consumers to interact with devices.

All of this new technology needs testing and a feedback loop for improvement. An Iceland-based startup, Treble, is positioning itself to be at the center of the voice AI industry by creating a simulation platform that can cater to model makers, robotics companies, and consumer hardware makers.

The company, founded in 2020 by acoustic engineers Finnur Pind and Jesper Pedersen, has raised $18 million in an extension of its Series A funding led by Paladin Capital Group, with participation from existing investors KOMPAS VC, Frumtak Ventures, EIC, and Omega ehf. It received an investment of $12 million in 2024, bringing its total raise to date to over $40 million. The startup counts Amazon and Logitech as customers.

body: The infamously tricky Elder Dragon was first introduced way back in Monster Hunter 2 in 2006, its penchanct for blast effects and flame breath pushing the PS2 tech quite hard at the time. Though the developer has made some pretty decent improvements to how the game runs since launch, it does seem that the beast's fiery attacks chew up the bitrate in the trailer a little. Here's hoping that isn't a reflection of the performance in-game.

One thing I did notice in this trailer is that the infamously tricky Teo fight looks even harder in the footage we've seen so far. Granted, the trailer is only three minutes-long (the real fight will probably take 10x that, in real-time), but it seems Capcom has given everyone's favourite exploding lion a little more utility than we saw in his last appearance in Monster Hunter Rise - Sunbreak.

body: In 2023, Metacore agreed to acquire 100% of Piñata, with the studio joining its operations to strengthen its in-house marketing and creative capabilities while working on Merge Mansion.
The studio has now announced its return as an independent business, describing the move as an opportunity to go back to its creative roots.

Piñata said it sees itself primarily as a team of visual storytellers, with its independent offering focused on creative storytelling across animation, illustration, visual development and user acquisition creatives.
“Throughout the years we've worked with the likes of Supercell, Rovio, Wooga, Housemarque, Zynga, and Moomin Characters," the team wrote in a post. “Now's the time to go back to our roots."

highlights.title: King Charles Makes Rare Statement Over Bombshell Memoir Claim He Told Diana’s Brother: “We’ll Forget Her Soon Enough”
highlights.summary: The Royal Family has, as the British press says, been dragged into a war of words with Charles Spencer, the younger brother of the beloved Princess Diana.
body: King Charles has, as the British press put it, been dragged into a “war of words” this week with Charles Spencer, the younger brother of the late Princess Diana.
Ahead of the release of Earl Spencer’s bombshell memoir about his sibling next week, titled Swan Song: Diana, My Sister, one particular claim from the book has seemingly thrown the Palace for a loop.

Such is the backlash that the Palace has made a rare public statement over the matter, where the firm appears to cast doubt on Spencer’s recollection of the event: “While we do not comment on books as a matter of principle, His Majesty is mindful that the pain of fraternal grief can cloud reason, affect judgment and colour memory in ways others do not recognise, even many years after such a loss,” it said, per BBC News.

The language, reporters have pointed out, is strikingly similar to Queen Elizabeth’s response to allegations of racism from Prince Harry and Meghan Markle in 2021, when she stated “recollections may vary,” in what was a surprisingly firm response from the monarch.

highlights.title: You be the judge: should my brother have told me the money I lent him was for his holiday?
highlights.summary: Ayaan thought she was lending money for something essential. Ahmed says the lender doesn’t get to dictate what it’s spent on. You decide who is on the money. • Find out how to get a disagreement settled or become a juror. I thought I was lending Ahmed money for something vital, not a trip to Greece.
body: My brother Ahmed and I both live at home – he’s 27 and I’m 25. I look up to him, but he’s much more disorganised than me, and over the years has asked me to keep secrets from our parents when he’s messed up. I lent him money recently, which he then used to go on holiday with his friends. It annoyed me, but I didn’t tell our parents.

Ahmed is between jobs right now. I am doing a journalism internship, but at least I have a wage. When Ahmed asked me for the money he didn’t say what it was for, but I assumed it was living expenses or something essential. Our parents work but send money home to family in Somalia, so we try to help out with the rent. Ahmed hasn’t been paying much recently but my parents don’t mind as they want him to find work. Also, I think that as the eldest son, he gets away with more.

Ahmed and I are close but we don’t talk in detail about our finances. I assumed that for him to have to ask me for money, it was vital. I lent him £400 a month or so ago, which is a lot out of my monthly internship pay of £1,500. We didn’t discuss terms or when he would repay me, but I thought it would be sooner rather than later.

body: The first few hires at a startup can define the company. But increasingly, not every new capability requires a new employee.

AI agents are beginning to take on engineering, customer support, research, and operational work that would previously have been assigned to early team members. For founders, that creates a new question before they even open a job requisition: What should people own, and what should be delegated to AI?

At TechCrunch Disrupt 2026, Josh Reeves, CEO and co-founder of Gusto; Michelle Johnson, senior vice president at Insight Partners; and John Koelliker, CEO and co-founder of Leland, come together on the Builders Stage for an insightful session called “Hiring When AI Is a Co-Founder.”

Join them at Moscone West in San Francisco, October 13–15, alongside 10,000+ startups, investors, and tech decision-makers exploring what it takes to build and scale the next generation of companies. highlights.title: OpenAI reveals cases of ‘concerning’ AI behaviour as it announces new disclosure system
highlights.summary: Model adopting ‘jailbreak-like instructions’ among cases as firm says it is introducing new way of tracking AI misalignment. OpenAI has disclosed six more examples of “unexpected or concerning” behaviour by its technology, as it warned the pace of development could not continue at “maximum speed…
body: In one of the new cases reported by OpenAI, an unreleased research model inserted “jailbreak-like instructions” into its own notes to disregard its normal constraints and told itself to be “freed from the roles and identities that bind other chatbots”.
In another instance, an AI agent uploaded files to the internet to obtain a browser citation without asking the user.

The San Francisco-based company behind ChatGPT said in a blogpost published on Wednesday night it was introducing a new framework for tracking, investigating and disclosing AI model misalignment, the term for AIs failing to adhere to human values and safety goals.

In the blogpost OpenAI echoed calls for a development slowdown issued by its archrival, Anthropic, which has said the current pace of growth poses an existential threat. “We do not believe that the AI industry has solved alignment and monitoring to a sufficient degree to continue responsibly scaling at maximum speed for much longer,” said OpenAI.

highlights.summary: It comes after Macklemore pledged $1m to Palestinian causes, challenging the tycoon to match the sum.
body: Robert Kraft, the US stadium owner who had pro-Palestinian rapper Macklemore removed as Ed Sheeran's opening act, says Sheeran asked him to match his own $2m (£1.5m) donation for "aid in the region".
It came after Macklemore said he would donate $1m (£750,000) to Palestinian organisations, challenging Kraft to match him.

Kraft, who owns the New England Patriots, wrote on Wednesday: "Earlier today, before Macklemore challenged me to match his donation, Ed called me and asked me to commit $2 million to match his donation to aid in the region to fight this humanitarian crisis.
"Ed now plans to reach out to other venue owners and our goal is to continue to work together to build bridges."

highlights.title: Hard parties, cheap rents and horrible flats: how 90s art and fashion redefined British culture
highlights.summary: An evocative new Tate Britain show captures an era when the UK’s newly flush creative industries teamed up with a generation of skint dreamers to bring the decade into vivid colour. Here is Kate Moss, with pink hair splayed across a pillow, her face scrubbed of makeup, her smile sweet and wonky.
body: These photos are old. They were taken a long time ago. But they’re young, too. They are curated by Edward Enninful for the Tate’s exhibition The 90s: Art and Fashion (Enninful worked at i-D in the 90s) and almost everyone involved is shiny and fresh. The models, whether professional or not, are mostly in their 20s, and the photographers are early in their careers. It gives the photos a youthful fizz, a verve. But the energy also comes from an understanding between photographer and subject. In many of the pictures you can feel the shared mischief, a “yes we’re serious about our ideas” but also a “look, we’re getting away with it!” delight.

Parties were plentiful. Aside from the club scene, magazines threw them, art galleries threw them, some random person that you met in a late-night drinking den said, “I know this place”, so you went. When you were out, you met artists, photographers, musicians, actors, writers, promoters, dealers, “entrepreneurs”. Often you had no idea what they did: I once walked into an office and realised that the esteemed head of design was the character with whom I’d spent a full-on all-nighter at Glastonbury a month before.

highlights.title: The streamers are fighting over Halloween
highlights.summary: The Toronto International Film Festival is a place to go to see the future of film, but this year it also provided a glimpse at what is coming very soon in the realm of streaming.
body: Crystal Lake, Carrie, Below, and Yaga are all competing in a very busy October.

Then there’s Peacock, which is joining the fray with a prequel series. Fans of Friday the 13th will know that Jason’s mom plays a pivotal role in the very first film, and the new show Crystal Lake explores how she got to that point. It stars Linda Cardellini as Pamela Voorhees, a single mother who is thrown into a pit of despair and disbelief when her young son drowns to death.

I went into the show thinking that I didn’t really need to know much more about the backstory of Jason’s mother, but the first two episodes that premiered at TIFF — and Cardellini’s performance in particular — have me second-guessing that. Crystal Lake is surprisingly tense and dramatic, but, given its connection to Friday the 13th, it also has slasher-movie levels of gore and gross-out deaths, ones that are so brutal they approach comedy. If nothing else, it gets off to a very strong start. All episodes of Crystal Lake hit Peacock on October 15th.

highlights.title: Washington Won’t Be Regulating AI Anytime Soon
highlights.summary: Even with mounting concerns about AI models going rogue, legislation appears unlikely, and the White House is outright opposed to oversight.
body: For weeks, Washington has been abuzz with talk of needing to push through some sort of AI regulation amid mounting concerns about the risks of highly capable frontier AI models going rogue.

But there is no reason to think any one measure can win the support of the White House, where officials have paused work on creating a FINRA-style regulatory body after President Donald Trump soured on the idea, or of Capitol Hill, where lawmakers have competing proposals that lack the votes to pass.

White House aides initially started sketching out a framework for an AI oversight agency connected to the administration soon after Google DeepMind’s cofounder Demis Hassabis floated the idea in a July 14 essay and in briefings to senior officials, according to sources familiar with the matter.

The Treasury Department and the White House’s Office of Science and Technology Policy envisioned a body where leading AI labs would self-regulate the development of frontier models, and they put together a preliminary draft to see what it could look like if executed.

highlights.title: PlayStation 5's latest firmware update takes Community Activity out of beta, but it's missing a key feature
highlights.summary: A new PlayStation 5 firmware update has officially arrived for everyone, after about a month of testing. The change log for firmware version 26.06-14.00.00 has changed in one major way since the beta first went live in August.
body: The Community Activity widget is now available for all players to add to their console's Welcome Hub. Community Activity wasn't part of the firmware's beta, but Sony has been testing the feature since May.

Community Activity has two views: Trending Now, and Top 10. Trending Now shows a list of 10 multiplayer games (or multiplayer modes within games) that are rising in popularity across PlayStation. This is where you can expect to see recently-updated games, hot new releases and games that got a sale bump. Each game tile also shows what pushed the game to get on that list, such as a surge in matches or hours played.

Top 10 is more straightforward, and it shows a list of the 10 most popular games over the last week. This ranking varies depending on your country or region, making it more accurate. You can probably expect these to be roughly the same week-to-week, though, if previous data is anything to go by. The only problem? Top 10 used to list player counts for each game in the beta, but that is gone from the final version.

highlights.title: The 2.5-hour AI-generated Odyssey movie is 2.5 hours too long
highlights.summary: Christopher Nolan's engrossing take on The Odyssey dominated at the box office and spurred a newfound interest in classic literature among filmgoers. But a new retelling of the story made entirely with AI is so bad that it might just make viewers hate the original tale altogether.
body: The movie is available to rent now for $9.99 and, as far as I can tell, you can only watch it via a web browser. In order to view it on my living room TV I had to mirror the screen from my phone, which is not exactly IMAX in 70mm. Things didn’t get much better once I pressed play.

The Fall is plagued by two main issues. The first is consistency. The world of the film is constantly morphing, to the point that it’s incredibly distracting. The height of the cyclops that traps Odysseus and his men changes from shot to shot, waves move in the opposite direction of the wind, mouths don’t match the words spoken (and sometimes they move without producing a sound at all), and oars bend and twist as sailors row. In one scene a huge fleet of boats is racing through the ocean and one of them is inexplicably moving sideways. The AI-produced voice-overs can be incomprehensible, and at various points the names of both Odysseus and Zeus are pronounced wrong.
points: Christopher Nolan's engrossing take on The Odyssey dominated at the box office and spurred a newfound interest in classic literature among filmgoers.

body: The Cricket Regulator had charged Leicestershire after the Grace Road pitch was rated as poor for last month’s win against Glamorgan. The cricket discipline panel has upheld the charge, leading to the deduction of the 19 points picked up for the victory plus eight more as a penalty. A Leicestershire statement said “the club is reviewing its position and considering all available options”, but the deduction left them bottom of the table, 38 points adrift of the last safe spot. With Hampshire 225 ahead with seven wickets standing, Leicestershire’s hopes in what is now a must-win match are slim.

Warwickshire flourish a 19-point hand on the table and wait after a second two-day victory in succession. Essex, further weakened by overnight substitutions to Shane Snater and Tom Westley, gave them the upper hand by conceding another 40 runs for the last wicket, thanks largely to an unbeaten 88 from Sam Hain. The Indian spinner Manav Suthar, with five for 75, and Chris Woakes, with three for 33, were too hot for Essex and Warwickshire easily knocked off the 133 needed.

highlights.title: Rachel Roddy’s recipe for rice, aubergine and mozzarella bake | A kitchen in Rome
highlights.summary: A 1950s cookbook classic – eat it hot and stringy or firm and flavoursome. Yesterday’s lunch and this week’s recipe is thanks to my friend, the designer Jake Tilson, who gave me a pristine 1977 edition of The Talisman Italian Cook Book.
body: I don’t regret making the recipe from page 161 for rice with aubergine, however, which I have adapted for variety’s sake. This bake is good when made with tinned tomatoes, but fresh ones bring a brighter burst of flavour. Ideally, try to get a mix of varieties – a few sweet cherries, a couple of plums, a big fleshy one – that have been peeled and cooked into a sweet-savoury sauce; if necessary, add a pinch of sugar.

A reason for eating this pretty much straight out of the oven and while it’s still steaming hot is the mozzarella, because the cheese is molten and pulls into those long strings that make serving it and eating it so entertaining. The benefit of waiting half an hour or longer is that the flavours develop, while the bake itself (and the mozzarella inside and on top) firms up. Or serve at whatever stage or temperature you like, with whatever variety of salad or vegetable.

Using a peeler, pare strips of skin from the aubergines so they are striped, then cut into 1cm-thick slices. Arrange these on an oiled baking tray, zigzag with more oil, sprinkle with salt, then bake at 180C (160C)/350F/gas 4 for 30-40 minutes, until tender and a little golden.

highlights.title: I Trained a Fly’s Brain to Generate WIRED Story Ideas
highlights.summary: I used an open-source map of a fruit fly’s brain to vibe code a website called PitchFly. Its headline suggestions were delightfully bananas.
body: He has 165,112 neurons, and they’re all trained to generate story ideas. A sampling of his early output: “The Hidden Weather Problem Inside Surveillance”; “The Engineers Who Think Elon Musk Needs Less Computer Security”; and my personal favorite, “Everyone Wants Cooking. Nobody Has Solved Donald Trump.”

PitchFly uses a detailed map of the brain of a male drosophila—the common fruit fly. Developed by researchers from Google and a number of academic institutions, the map, known as a connectome, captures the way that 166,000 neurons and 125 million connecting synapses fire in response to stimuli. In essence, you can use it to simulate how a fly would respond to lots of stuff—it’s a very simple version of artificial intelligence based on charting real biological intelligence.

In the future, perhaps I could have the program continue to learn by reading new WIRED headlines. For now, though, this seems like a decent proof of concept, not to mention evidence at last that the average WIRED writer is intellectually superior to a fruit fly.
After the connectome’s release in early September, dozens of other weird and wonderful projects powered by fruit-fly intelligence sprang up.

body: London Fashion Week (LFW) is fast approaching, and the schedule is tight, bolstered with a slew of activations, parties and dinners. Comparative to New York, it’s a lighter load, but the mix of big-ticket shows and emerging independents — many eschewing the runway format for experiential events — continues to position the city as a springboard for hot, young talent and heritage stalwarts.

“We are opening up London Fashion Week to new energy, new ideas and new ways of engaging with fashion,” says Laura Weir, the British Fashion Council's CEO. “Alongside traditional catwalk formats, the schedule features everything from [Californian brand] 5000’s multisensory sound bath to AllSaints ’s zine launch. That breadth is deliberate. London Fashion Week is a global platform for designers and businesses, but it is also a way of demonstrating the wider cultural and economic value of fashion. By bringing together fashion, art, music, technology, retail, and culture, we are demonstrating the sector’s reach, relevance and ability to create value far beyond the catwalk.”
